bridge: M03 introduced counting. Use a fictional population so every percentage can be turned back into a count.
teaching:
### Start with how common the problem is

Suppose one out of every thousand events is malicious. That is the base rate: how common the condition is before considering a particular alert. A detector can look accurate and still raise many harmless alerts when malicious events are rare.

Sensitivity asks how many malicious events are detected. A false-positive rate asks how many harmless events incorrectly raise an alert. These percentages use different groups underneath the fraction.

### Choose the right denominator

“Among malicious events, how many alerted?” differs from “Among alerts, how many are malicious?” Build a two-by-two count table before dividing. Bayes' rule expresses how evidence changes a probability; the table makes the same bookkeeping visible for small examples.

### Check independence

Two observations are independent when learning one does not change the probability of the other under the model. Two alerts produced by the same underlying rule may not be independent evidence. Multiplying their probabilities without checking can exaggerate certainty.

### Understand entropy in context

Entropy measures uncertainty under a probability distribution. A uniformly random choice among many possibilities can have high entropy. A long password chosen through a predictable habit may have much less uncertainty than its length suggests. Name the selection process, not just the character count.

### Understand the birthday scale

Collision probability asks whether any two choices match, not whether one choice matches one fixed target. Among q choices there are \(q(q-1)/2\) pairs to compare. For uniformly random values from N possibilities, collisions therefore become appreciable around the birthday scale of \(\sqrt N\) choices, not N. This approximation needs its stated sampling assumptions; it is not a guarantee that a collision occurs at one exact count.

### Calculate alert precision and recall

TP means a real incident that alerted; FP means a harmless event that alerted; FN means a real incident that was missed; TN means a harmless event that did not alert. Precision is \(TP/(TP+FP)\): among alerts, how many were real? Recall is \(TP/(TP+FN)\): among real incidents, how many did we find? Fill the count table before using the formulas. A zero denominator needs an explicit handling rule rather than ordinary division.
example:
Population: 10,000 events
Real incidents: 100; benign: 9,900
Detector catches 90 incidents and alerts on 99 benign events.
                  alert  no alert
incident            90       10
benign              99     9801
Precision = 90/(90+99) ≈ 47.6%
Recall    = 90/(90+10) = 90%
explanation: Read one row at a time. There are 100 real incidents: 90 alerted and 10 did not. There are 9,900 benign events: 99 alerted and 9,801 did not. The row totals add to 10,000, so no event is missing. The alert column has \(90+99=189\) events. Of those, 90 are true incidents, giving precision \(90/189\approx0.476=47.6\%\). For recall, keep the incident row: \(90/(90+10)=90\%\). The detector finds many incidents, yet more than half its alerts concern benign events. That happens because benign events are much more common. Choosing whether this burden is acceptable requires the costs of review and missed incidents, not a single “accuracy” slogan.
exercise: Use a second population: 1,000 events, 20 incidents, 15 detected incidents and 35 false alerts. Fill all four matrix cells, calculate precision and recall, and state the number of missed incidents. For a uniformly random 24-bit value, estimate the birthday collision scale. Explain why it is smaller than the number of available values.
solution: Start with the incident row: 20 incidents minus 15 detected gives 5 misses, so TP=15 and FN=5. There are \(1000-20=980\) benign events; subtract the 35 false alerts to get TN=945. All four cells sum to 1000. All alerts total \(15+35=50\), so precision is \(15/50=30\%\). All incidents total 20, so recall is \(15/20=75\%\). If your denominators are reversed, restate the question in words before recalculating. For 24 bits, \(\sqrt{2^{24}}=2^{12}=4096\) draws is the birthday scale. Many pairs are being compared, so a repeat can become plausible long before all \(2^{24}\) values are used.
challenge: A detector is applied to 100 events, including 10 incidents. It catches 8 incidents and alerts on 18 benign events. Calculate precision, recall and total alerts. Explain why independent trials would be an unsafe assumption for repeated events from one device.
challenge_solution: Precision=8/26≈30.8%; recall=80%; alerts=26. Events from one device may share configuration or a single incident and be correlated. Treating them as independent can overstate the amount of evidence.
